title: Product Design: Design a Product for a User Segment
prompt: Design a product to help recent immigrants build credit history in a new country. Walk me through how you'd approach it — who you'd build for, what you'd build, and why.
blurb: A product-sense case — pick a user, uncover real needs and pain points, prioritize a solution, and reason about tradeoffs and success.

rubric.label: User empathy
rubric.description: Segments the broad user group, picks a specific target, and articulates their goals, contexts, and concrete pain points from the user's point of view — not generic personas.

rubric.label: Prioritization
rubric.description: Generates multiple solution ideas, then narrows to a focused MVP using an explicit rationale (impact vs effort, severity of pain, reach) rather than trying to build everything.

rubric.label: Solution & product thinking
rubric.description: Proposes a concrete, coherent solution that maps directly to the chosen user's top pain point, and describes the core experience end to end.

rubric.label: Success metrics
rubric.description: Defines what success looks like with a clear primary metric tied to the user goal, plus guardrail/counter metrics.

rubric.label: Tradeoffs & risks
rubric.description: Surfaces the key tradeoffs (e.g. inclusivity vs risk, speed vs trust), regulatory/abuse risks, and how they'd validate the riskiest assumption.

rubric.label: Communication & structure
rubric.description: Lays out a clear structure (user -> needs -> solutions -> prioritize -> metrics/tradeoffs), signposts, and stays organized under follow-ups.

reference.scenario: Open-ended product-design prompt. There is no single right product; the interviewer assesses whether the candidate structures the problem, grounds the design in a real user need, prioritizes, and reasons about metrics and tradeoffs. Context the candidate should surface themselves: recent immigrants often arrive with no domestic credit file, so they're locked out of housing, phone plans, car loans, and cards despite being creditworthy abroad; they may lack an SSN initially, distrust or not understand the local credit system, and face language barriers. Sub-segments differ sharply: students, skilled-visa workers with income, refugees/asylees with little income, family-reunification arrivals. Good candidates pick ONE segment and design for its specific pain. Plausible solutions: a secured card or 'credit-builder' account that reports rent/utility/telecom payments to bureaus; leveraging alternative or cross-border credit data; a deposit-backed card that graduates to unsecured. Real tensions: inclusivity vs default risk, regulatory/KYC constraints, trust-building with a wary user, and unit economics on a thin-file, low-balance population.
model_points: Clarify the goal and constraints briefly: business objective (new user acquisition? a fintech's growth? social impact?), geography, and what 'build credit' concretely means (a bureau-reported credit file).

Segment the user group and pick one target with a reason: e.g. skilled-visa workers with steady income but no domestic file — high intent, monetizable, and a sharply defined pain — versus students or refugees whose needs and economics differ.
Articulate that segment's top pain points from their view: 'I earn well but get denied for an apartment/card because I have no history here, and I don't understand how to start.'

Brainstorm several solutions (secured/credit-builder card, rent & utility payment reporting, cross-border credit-history import, education + guided onboarding), then prioritize to a focused MVP using impact vs effort and pain severity.

Describe the MVP end to end: e.g. a credit-builder card backed by a small deposit that reports on-time payments to the bureaus and graduates the user to unsecured, with plain-language onboarding that explains how credit works.

Define success: primary metric = users who establish a scored credit file / graduate to unsecured within N months; guardrails = default/charge-off rate, and a trust/comprehension metric (activation, NPS).

Name the key tradeoffs and risks — inclusivity vs default risk, KYC/regulatory limits, unit economics on low balances — and state the single riskiest assumption and how you'd test it (e.g. a pilot measuring whether reported payments actually lift scores and whether defaults stay acceptable).

probes.trigger: candidate jumps to a solution before choosing a user
probes.question: Who exactly is this for? These users are not one group — pick a segment and tell me why that one.
Put yourself in that user's shoes on day one in the country — what's the single most painful moment, and does your product hit it?

probes.trigger: candidate tries to build many features
probes.question: If you could ship only one thing first, what is it and why — what's your prioritization rationale?
How would you know this product is working? What's your primary metric, and what guardrail would stop you from gaming it?
You're extending credit to thin-file users. What's the tension between being inclusive and managing default, and how do you handle it?
What is the riskiest assumption in this design, and how would you validate it before a full build?

red_flags: Jumps straight to a feature/solution without choosing or understanding a user
Treats 'immigrants' as one homogeneous group with generic needs
No prioritization — proposes a laundry list with no MVP or rationale
No success metrics, or a vanity metric with no guardrail
Ignores tradeoffs, regulatory/abuse risk, or default economics entirely
Rambling and unstructured; can't tie the solution back to a specific user pain
follow_ups: How would your design change if the target were students with little or no income instead of salaried workers?
Rent-reporting depends on landlords and bureaus cooperating — how would you de-risk that dependency?
If early data showed users open the account but never use it, how would you diagnose and respond?
How would you balance a mission of financial inclusion against a P&L that punishes defaults?
reference.exemplar_answer: A strong candidate first clarifies the goal (say, a fintech growing a creditworthy but underserved base) and what 'build credit' means (a bureau-reported file), then segments: students, skilled-visa earners, refugees, family reunification. They pick skilled-visa workers — steady income, high intent, monetizable, sharply defined pain — and voice that pain: 'I earn well but I'm denied apartments and cards because I have no domestic history, and no one explains how to start.' They brainstorm secured cards, rent/utility reporting, cross-border history import, and guided education, then prioritize to an MVP: a small-deposit credit-builder card that reports on-time payments to the bureaus and graduates users to unsecured, wrapped in plain-language onboarding. They set a primary metric (share who reach a scored file / graduate within ~6 months), guardrails (charge-off rate, activation/comprehension), and name the core tension — inclusivity versus default risk under KYC constraints and thin-file economics. They close by identifying the riskiest assumption (that reported payments meaningfully lift scores without unacceptable defaults) and proposing a small pilot to test it before scaling. Throughout they keep a clear structure and connect every decision back to the chosen user.

interviewer_notes: This is a product-sense / product-design case; the mid bar is user-first structure, a chosen segment, a prioritized MVP, and at least a basic metrics + tradeoffs story. Do NOT let the candidate design for 'everyone' — if they don't pick a segment, push them to. Reward brainstorming breadth followed by disciplined narrowing with an explicit rationale (impact vs effort). Probe for the primary metric plus a guardrail. The strongest signal is naming the riskiest assumption and a way to validate it. Keep them structured; interrupt rambling with 'who is this for again, and what's their top pain?' Reserve the last minutes for one tradeoff/risk follow-up.
